summary: Undo for the shell. A content-addressed history of a working tree (src/chronicle.rs), fed by snapshots, by `proteus run` and by a file watcher (src/watch.rs). Restore and undo are dry runs unless --apply, and never overwrite or delete a file whose content is not already in the store. Built at 5de467c; attacked in two review passes (0b23461 and 1e5cc03; then bdf261a, 8967ed4 and the commit that brings this text), each fix with a test that failed before it.

done.what: History of a folder under <data>\chronicle\<name>-<id>: file contents and folder listings stored once each, named by their SHA-256, in append-only pack files with an index that can be rebuilt from the packs; an append-only log of snapshots {tree, times, time, label, parent, reason} and steps {kind, command, exit code, duration, tree before, tree after}; a lock file held by whoever is writing
done.evidence: tests the_same_content_is_stored_once_and_text_is_deflated, the_store_survives_a_lost_index_and_a_torn_pack (index deleted, a half-written record at the end of the pack, an index cut mid-record, a log cut mid-line, one byte of a stored file flipped: all read back or refused correctly). Under test a pack is closed at 256 KB, so the ordinary tests read and repair across several packs. Review: 24 processes at once on one store (12 snapshots, 6 runs, 6 status, a watch running): all exit 0, 26 log entries numbered without a gap, every one of the 20 trees loads

done.what: A record found in a pack that the index never named (its writer stopped before the index was written) is read through and checked against its hash before a writer adopts it. One that fails is passed over, and cut off if nothing sound follows it. Before, it was believed on the word of its header: after a power cut (header and length on disk, zeros where the content should be) the store answered 'already there' for that content for ever and every later tree naming it could not be brought back
done.evidence: test a_record_whose_content_never_reached_the_disk_is_not_believed (failed at 1e5cc03). Cost, measured: a snapshot after the whole index was deleted (24,199 objects read and checked, index rebuilt) 702-726 ms wall against 152-156 with the index in place

done.what: A tree id is the SHA-256 of the root folder's listing; a listing names each file by content hash, size and attributes and each folder by the hash of its own listing. One id fixes every file below it. A one-file change stores one listing per folder on its path, not a listing of the whole tree
done.evidence: test any_recorded_tree_can_be_brought_back_exactly compares every tree id with one computed by separate code (own walk, own hashing)

done.what: An unchanged file is not read again: per file the cache keeps size, modified time, change time and the volume's file id, taken from the folder listing (no file is opened). A file rewritten with its old size and its modified time put back (SetFileTime), and another file of equal size and time moved onto the path, are both seen. Files written in the last 2 s are read again next time. A file with more than one name (hard links) is read every time: Windows keeps the listing up to date only for the name a file was written through
done.evidence: tests an_unchanged_tree_is_not_read_again_and_a_sly_change_is_still_seen, a_change_made_through_another_name_of_a_file_is_seen (first review pass, which reports it failing at 5de467c); a warm snapshot reads 0 of 10,000 files. What gets past the cache is under known_issues (mapped writes, a change time put back)

done.what: Ignored: what git ignores (.gitignore at every level with ! rules, .git/info/exclude, the global file; letter case ignored as git does on Windows), plus .proteusignore, plus .git/.hg/.svn/.jj and the store itself. Ignored files are never captured, restored or deleted
done.evidence: test what_git_ignores_is_what_chronicle_ignores: a repository made by the real git with 30 files, three nested .gitignore files and a private exclude file; chronicle's tree holds exactly the files `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard` lists. Test ignored_files_are_neither_captured_nor_deleted

done.what: `chronicle restore TREE` makes the folder equal a recorded tree; `chronicle undo [--step N]` puts back what one step changed, where the folder still is as that step left it. Both print the exact plan and change nothing unless --apply; with --apply the current state is snapshotted first and the whole thing is recorded as a step, so it can itself be undone. A file changed after the step ended is reported as a conflict and left alone unless --force. Plain `undo` takes the last step that changed anything and says which steps it passed over; doing nothing records no step. Exit code 3 when --apply could not do everything
done.evidence: tests any_recorded_tree_can_be_brought_back_exactly (240 random creates, edits, deletes, renames, folder moves, attribute and type changes, a snapshot after each; then all 241 trees restored in shuffled order and compared byte for byte with an in-memory copy), undo_leaves_later_changes_alone_unless_forced, run_then_undo_then_undo_again, long_paths_round_trip_and_a_dry_run_writes_nothing, files_deeper_than_260_characters_are_replaced_made_and_deleted. Review, with the real exe in temp folders: a 588-character path edited, removed, added, restored, undone and restored from nothing; a file renamed only in letter case restored and undone three times over; conflicts on an edited and on a deleted-and-recreated file, left alone, then forced, then the forced undo undone

done.what: A dry run looks at the disk for everything --apply would refuse and lists it; the same plan is what --apply carries out. Listed beforehand: a link on the way to a path, something outside the tree where a file or folder should go, a file another program holds open (for writing, or in a way that lets nobody replace it), a file whose content is missing from the store, a folder that cannot be emptied (ignored files, a link), a folder a program is using (a shell whose current folder it is). A folder that stays makes the result not complete
done.evidence: tests a_dry_run_names_everything_apply_will_refuse (six obstacles at once; the first review pass reports it failing at 5de467c), a_dry_run_names_a_folder_that_a_shell_is_sitting_in (a real cmd.exe with the folder as its current folder; failed at 1e5cc03: the dry run promised `remove-folder build`, --apply kept it and reported not verified), a_dry_run_names_content_the_store_no_longer_has (failed at 1e5cc03), a_folder_renamed_only_in_letter_case_comes_back_with_what_it_holds

done.what: `proteus run [--rehash] -- CMD ARGS...`: snapshot, run the command with this console and its own stdio, snapshot again, record command line, exit code, duration and both trees as one step; exits with the command's exit code. If the state before cannot be recorded the command is not run (exit 125); if the state after cannot, the command's own exit code is still returned and stderr says the step is missing. `npm` finds `npm.cmd` (PATHEXT). --rehash reads every file before and after instead of going by sizes and times
done.evidence: tests run_then_undo_then_undo_again, a_command_keeps_its_exit_code_when_its_step_cannot_be_recorded, a_write_through_a_mapped_view_is_recorded_when_every_file_is_read (review: a real program writes one byte through a memory-mapped view; with --rehash the step holds both states and undo puts back the first; with the flag off the same test fails, the step records 0 modified); gate step 'chronicle' (forge/chronicle.ps1) with the real exe: run (exit 7) -> undo -> undo again -> restore, folder identical each time. Review: Ctrl+Break sent to `proteus run` and its command in their own process group (cmd running waitfor): the command stopped, proteus waited for it, took the snapshot after and recorded the step (3 files added), exiting 91 ms after the break

done.what: Restore and undo never destroy what the store does not hold: at the moment a file is replaced or deleted it is opened so that nothing can be writing to it and read through; unless it is byte for byte what the snapshot taken first captured, it is left alone. Links are never followed (symbolic links and junctions are listed and skipped; every folder on the way to a write is checked). Paths are checked on capture and again on restore: no `..`, absolute paths, drive letters, UNC, alternate data streams, device names, trailing dots or spaces. Drives, the user profile (or anything holding it) and PROTEUS's own data folder cannot be tracked; a tree over its budget (default 200,000 files, 8,192 MB) is refused before anything is read. Locked or unreadable files are recorded as failures in the tree itself, so no tree pretends they were absent
done.evidence: tests a_junction_is_reported_and_never_followed, symbolic_links_are_reported_and_never_written_through, a_hand_made_tree_cannot_reach_outside_the_root (16 bad names x 3 line kinds written into the store by hand, and plans handed straight to the code that touches the disk), a_file_another_program_is_writing_is_never_replaced, restore_never_destroys_what_the_store_does_not_hold, a_locked_file_is_recorded_as_a_failure_and_nothing_stops, drives_the_profile_and_proteus_own_data_are_never_tracked, the_budget_is_checked_before_anything_is_stored. 0 SKIPPED lines in `cargo test --release -- --nocapture` (symbolic links, git, hard links, icacls and powershell were all available). Review, with the real exe: 12 hand-made listings appended to a pack and named in the log (..\victim, ../victim, .., an absolute path, C:evil.txt, a UNC path, a named stream, NUL, a trailing dot, a trailing space, a folder named .., an attribute bit outside r/h/s): each refused by the dry run and by --apply (exit 1), the file beside the root untouched. A junction, a folder symlink and a file symlink pointing outside, made before tracking: listed, nothing from behind them in the packs. A tracked folder and a tracked file swapped for links between snapshots: restore refused those three paths (exit 3), the folder outside byte for byte as before. Files named NUL, con.txt, `trail.`, `trail ` and a folder named prn (made through \\?\ paths): each recorded as not captured, none touched by restore

done.what: Every file restore writes is written under a temporary name beside its path (.proteus-restore-<pid>-<n>.tmp) and moved in whole, so a path never holds half a file. A file that is replaced keeps its permissions, named streams and creation time (ReplaceFile, with the old file held open the whole time). Temporary files a killed restore leaves are reported by status and by a dry run, and removed by the next snapshot or --apply. A file whose deletion fails at the last moment keeps the read-only, hidden and system bits it had
done.evidence: tests a_replaced_file_keeps_its_permissions_and_named_streams, a_new_file_appears_at_its_path_only_when_it_is_whole, what_an_interrupted_restore_left_behind_is_reported_then_removed, many_files_go_back_into_folders_that_are_gone (the first review pass reports each as failing at 5de467c; the second did not run them there), a_file_that_could_not_be_deleted_after_all_keeps_its_attributes (failed at 8967ed4: the file was left writable and visible). done.what: When each file was last written is recorded with every snapshot, beside the tree and not in its id (same shape as the tree, so untouched folders cost nothing). `chronicle diff` shows it

src/watch.rs: file changes from the OS as a Rust API (watch::Watcher { events: crossbeam Receiver<Event>, counters }). One thread blocked in ReadDirectoryChangesW (recursive, overlapped, 256 KB buffer, 64 KB on a share); create, modify, delete, rename {from}; an overflow arrives as Rescan. The event queue is bounded (65,536): a consumer that stops reading makes the OS buffer overflow instead of this process grow
done.evidence: watch tests: sees_create_modify_rename_and_delete, overflow_is_reported_and_the_watch_goes_on (10,000 files unread into a 4 KB buffer: Rescan delivered, later changes still arrive), ten_thousand_changes_with_the_default_buffer_lose_nothing_silently, stops_promptly_and_reports_a_missing_root

done.what: `proteus chronicle watch [DIR]`: captures after changes have been quiet for --debounce ms (default 200; at the latest 2 s after the first). Changes under ignored folders, .git and the store cause no capture. Costs nothing while nothing changes

known_issues: Typed at a PowerShell prompt with nothing piped, `proteus run` is not waited for: the prompt returns at once, $LASTEXITCODE is empty and the command's output arrives afterwards (seen by builder and review in a real pseudo-terminal, rendered with `proteus shot`: forge/lanes/chronicle/unpiped.ps1). The exe is a windowed program and PowerShell does not wait for those. It does wait, and the exit code is right (7 of 7), through `cmd /c`, with `| Out-Host`, with Start-Process -Wait, and from any program that starts it and waits (the gate, an agent's subprocess call). The same is true of every other proteus subcommand.

A snapshot goes by each file's size, times and file id, and two kinds of write leave those as they were (measured, see what_a_snapshot_cannot_see). One made through a memory-mapped view (a database, a numeric array kept on disk): never seen by `snap`, by `watch` (no event arrives) or by a plain `proteus run`, however long afterwards, until something else changes the file. One by a program that puts the change time back as well as the modified time. For both, `snap --rehash` and `proteus run --rehash` read every file and see it. What a plain step gets wrong then: it records 'nothing changed', and the next step records a state before that was never on disk, so undoing that next step puts back the older content. Restore is not fooled into destroying anything (it reads the file before replacing it).

A write handed to Windows through a handle that stays open (a log being appended, a database) is not seen by a snapshot or by the watcher until that program closes the file or flushes it to disk: until then the folder's listing still shows the old size and times. Measured by the builder and again by the review: an append and a same-size overwrite, each left unflushed with the handle open, were missed by every snapshot until the handle closed (the review waited 3 s for the overwrite and 9 s for the append) and captured by the first snapshot after; a write followed by a flush to disk was seen while the handle was still open. (In one run the appended size did show up early: the measuring script itself had asked Windows for the file's length in between.) After a `proteus run` command exits its own files are closed, so this concerns programs it leaves running.

Every snapshot lists the whole tree: about 45-70 ms per 5,000 folders plus 25-35 ms. `proteus run` therefore adds two snapshots and a process start to every command (264-371 ms against 18-26 on the 10,000-file tree; 598 with --rehash), and `watch` records a change about 110-140 ms after its debounce. Neither is proportional to what changed.

The store only grows. There is no command to drop old snapshots or reclaim space, and no command that re-reads a whole store to check it (content is checked against its hash whenever it is read for a restore, and when a writer adopts a record the index did not name).

What is captured is file content and the read-only, hidden and system bits. Not captured, so not restored: links (symbolic links and junctions are listed and skipped), alternate data streams, permissions, creation times, the compressed/encrypted/sparse state, and whether two names are hard links to one file (they come back as two files). A file that is replaced keeps its own permissions and streams; one that was deleted and is brought back has its folder's. Restored files carry the time of the restore, by design.
Ignored files are outside history: undo does not bring back an ignored file a command deleted, and a folder that should be removed is kept if ignored files are still in it (the dry run says so).

A file that could not be read (locked, access denied, a cloud placeholder not downloaded, a name Windows reserves such as NUL or one ending in a dot or space) is recorded as not captured; restoring to that tree leaves it as it is and says so, and a restore never overwrites a file it cannot read first.

A dry run cannot foresee everything. Not foreseen, and reported only by --apply (as failed, exit 3): a file that is a running program, and content that is in the store but damaged (that is known only when it is read). Anything that changes between the dry run and --apply is, as it must be, found at the last moment.
Any file named exactly like restore's own temporary files (.proteus-restore-<digits>-<digits>.tmp) is taken for a leftover: left out of every tree and removed by the next snapshot.

Command lines are kept in the log exactly as given, and file contents are kept as plain copies, under the data folder, readable by anything that can read that folder. A password passed as an argument to `proteus run` is in the log. Files a project keeps out of git by .gitignore are not captured; anything else is, secrets included.

Two `proteus run` commands at once in one folder each record the other's changes as part of their own step (the lock is not held while a command runs). The log stays sound (24 processes at once: no gap, every tree loads), but undoing one such step undoes what both did to the files it touched.

Ctrl+Break during `proteus run` was exercised by the review (the command stopped, proteus waited, the step was recorded). A real Ctrl+C typed in a terminal goes through the same handler and has not been tried: no way was found to send one to a process group from outside.

Not tried, expected from how Windows works: started by a program that has no console at all (a windowed launcher, a detached service), `proteus run` starts a console command that has no console to inherit, and Windows gives that command a console window of its own. From a terminal, a shell, an agent's shell tool or inside PROTEUS there is a console and nothing opens. It was not tried because doing so would open a window on a machine someone is typing on.

Only NTFS on a local disk has been exercised. FAT/exFAT (no change time, unstable file ids), ReFS, network shares (the 64 KB watcher buffer fallback) and folders with per-directory case sensitivity are untested.
A pack file is closed at 1 GiB and a new one begun. That path runs in the tests with the limit lowered to 256 KB; the largest store made holds 602 MB in one pack.
The history of a folder is found by its path: a folder that is moved or renamed starts a new history. The old one stays on disk.

Restore is atomic per file, not per tree: if the process is killed part-way the folder is part old, part new. Nothing is lost (the state before was snapshotted, and is the last entry in the log) and running the restore again finishes it; the review killed one and saw exactly that. The partial restore is not a step, so `undo` does not know of it: go back with `restore` and the tree of that last entry.
The object index (64 bytes per object) and the log are read whole by every command. Measured up to 36,320 objects; the default budget of 200,000 files has not been tried.

Between the check that a folder is not a link and the write into it there is no lock: a program that swaps a folder for a junction in that instant is not defended against. The same instant exists between a file being checked and its being deleted by name: a program that moves the checked file away and puts another at its path in that instant would lose the other. (While a file is replaced it is held open, and no writer can reach it.)

The first snapshot of files that have never been read since they were written is slow on this machine (8.6-11.3 s against 0.5-0.7 s for the same 10,000 files), as is any first read of them by any program.
Errors are plain text on stderr with exit code 1 even under --json; only results are JSON.

user_notes: One thing departs from the brief on purpose: a file's modified time is not part of the tree id and is not put back on restore. It is recorded with every snapshot beside the tree. Reason: if it were in the id, touching a file would make a new tree and no restore could ever reach an old id without also putting old times back; and putting old times back makes cargo and make believe a restored file was not changed, so they keep the build of the newer source. Restored files are written 'now', as `git checkout` does.

A second departure: the listing is one per folder (each naming its sub-folders by hash) rather than one flat list for the whole tree. A flat list of 10,000 files is about 1.3 MB to store again for every one-file change.

To use it: `proteus chronicle track` in a project (asks nothing, refuses drives and your profile folder), then either wrap commands as `proteus run -- <command>` or leave `proteus chronicle watch` running; `proteus chronicle undo` shows what it would do and `--apply` does it. From a PowerShell prompt use `cmd /c proteus run -- ...` or add `| Out-Host` until the console front exists (see known_issues).

For a command that writes through memory-mapped files (a database, numpy arrays kept on disk) use `proteus run --rehash -- <command>`: without it that step, and the one after it, are not exact. It costs a read of every file twice (0.6 s instead of 0.3 s on the 10,000-file tree).
Nothing starts it for you yet: no window or daemon runs the watcher, and commands typed in a session are not steps unless wrapped.
Ignored files are not history. If your build output or .env is in .gitignore, undo will not bring it back.
If undo says a folder stays because a program is using it, a shell is probably sitting in it: leave the folder and run the undo again.
